title: Generalizing Cross-Document Event Coreference Resolution Across Multiple Corpora
research_question: How well do cross-document event-coreference systems and their learned signals generalize across heterogeneous corpora, and can multi-corpus evaluation and training improve robustness?
methodology: The authors establish a uniform evaluation across ECB+, GVC, and a token-level reannotation of FCC called FCC-T. They compare a corpus-independent feature-based mention-pair system with a recent neural event-coreference model and analyze which action, participant, temporal, spatial, and contextual features matter in each corpus. They then train systems on individual and combined corpora and test cross-corpus transfer using coreference metrics including LEA and CoNLL measures. Model behavior and dataset structure are also inspected to identify sources of corpus-specific overfitting.

key_findings.finding: Systems trained on a single event-coreference corpus suffer substantial performance degradation when evaluated on unseen corpora.
ECB+ can be modeled largely from event-action information, while FCC-T and GVC require a more balanced use of time, participants, and other contextual signals.
The feature-based approach has lower peak performance in some settings but behaves more consistently across corpora than the evaluated neural system.
Design choices tailored to ECB+, including exploiting its document-link distribution through preclustering, can overfit that corpus and generalize poorly elsewhere.
Joint training on FCC-T and GVC obtains a harmonic-mean LEA F1 of 40.9 across the evaluated corpora, more than 4.5 points above the best corresponding single-corpus training result.
The experiments support evaluating cross-document event-coreference systems on multiple corpora rather than treating strong performance on one benchmark as evidence of general robustness.

limitations: The empirical study is restricted to the news domain.
The evaluated corpora each contain fewer than one thousand documents, far below the scale of many real document streams.
The available corpora do not permit a meaningful investigation of event-coreference links across unrelated topic partitions.
The study evaluates three corpora and a limited set of system architectures, so conclusions about all possible modeling approaches remain bounded by that setup.
The authors do not demonstrate the effect of improved cross-document event coreference on downstream applications.
Incomplete event-mention annotation in existing corpora complicates end-to-end event-detection evaluation.
raw_claims: Prior cross-document event-coreference systems were commonly developed and evaluated on only one corpus.
The study compares ECB+, GVC, and the reannotated FCC-T corpus under a uniform setup.
Event-action similarity dominates prediction on ECB+ more strongly than on the other two datasets.
Time and participant information are more important on FCC-T and GVC.
Single-corpus models generally transfer poorly to unseen datasets.
A simpler feature-based model is more stable across corpora than the evaluated neural model.
Some ECB+-specific modeling choices exploit structural properties that do not transfer reliably.
Training on FCC-T and GVC together improves aggregate robustness across corpora.
The authors recommend multi-corpus evaluation for future cross-document event-coreference systems.
The released resources include data, annotation guidelines, and a system implementation.
